props.title: PixiJS Filters & Post-Processing Shaders
props.subtitle: GPU-accelerated visual effects, custom fragment shaders, and the FilterSystem architecture

what.definition: PixiJS Filters are post-processing shader programs that intercept the rendering of a DisplayObject or Container, capture its output into an offscreen RenderTarget, and execute GPU fragment shaders to transform pixels.
what.summary: A powerful effects subsystem in PixiJS that enables blurs, color grading, displacement maps, glows, outlines, and custom GLSL/WGSL shaders with automatic bounding box padding and render target pooling.
bullets: Post-Processing Pipeline: Intercepts display tree rendering into offscreen framebuffers
Built-in & Community Filters: Blur, ColorMatrix, Displacement, Noise, Glow, Outline, Shockwave
Custom GLSL Shaders: Write custom vertex and fragment shaders with animated uniforms
FilterSystem & Resource Pooling: Reusable RenderTarget pools to prevent VRAM memory churn

why.summary: Standard 2D sprite rendering is limited to linear tinting and alpha blending. Creating atmospheric effects like heat distortion, bloom, chromatic aberration, or dynamic drop shadows requires per-pixel fragment manipulation.
why.impact: PixiJS Filters provide hardware-accelerated post-processing without writing complex framebuffer ping-pong pipelines from scratch, giving 2D games and web applications studio-grade visual polish.

terms.shortDefinition: The core PixiJS rendering subsystem that coordinates filter stacks, offscreen targets, and shader passes.
terms.detailedDefinition: FilterSystem manages the lifecycle of filter execution. When a filtered container is drawn, FilterSystem computes padded bounding rectangles, pushes temporary RenderTargets, executes shader passes, and composites pixels to the target destination.
terms.whyItMatters: Abstracts low-level WebGL framebuffer binding, viewport scaling, and multi-pass ping-pong buffer management into a clean declarative API.

dialogue.user: How does PixiJS know when to draw to an offscreen buffer?
dialogue.aiThoughts: Explain the FilterSystem push/pop interception mechanism.
dialogue.aiQuestion: When the renderer encounters an object with `filters.length > 0`, it calls `filterSystem.push()` to redirect child drawing into a temporary RenderTarget.

terms.shortDefinition: A reusable pool of GPU framebuffers and textures used for intermediate offscreen filter rendering.
terms.detailedDefinition: Creating WebGL textures and framebuffers dynamically causes severe garbage collection pauses and GPU memory fragmentation. PixiJS maintains a pool of RenderTargets, leasing them during filter passes and recycling them immediately after.
terms.whyItMatters: Prevents VRAM allocation churn and ensures consistent 60 FPS performance during heavy post-processing effects.

dialogue.user: Does applying filters create new GPU textures every single frame?
dialogue.aiThoughts: Clarify RenderTarget pooling vs fresh allocation.
dialogue.aiQuestion: No! PixiJS borrows existing RenderTargets from its internal pool and returns them immediately after shader compositing.

terms.shortDefinition: A GPU program executed for every pixel to compute color, alpha, and visual transformations.
terms.detailedDefinition: In PixiJS filters, the fragment shader receives the offscreen texture via the uniform `uSampler` and texture coordinates via `vTextureCoord`. It calculates per-pixel colors using math algorithms (e.g. convolutions, color matrices, noise functions).
terms.whyItMatters: Provides total per-pixel artistic control, enabling real-time lighting, distortion, bloom, and stylized rendering.

dialogue.user: What is the primary input to a filter fragment shader?
dialogue.aiThoughts: Identify the sampler and coordinate uniforms.
dialogue.aiQuestion: The offscreen texture `uSampler` containing the rendered display object, sampled at `vTextureCoord`!

terms.shortDefinition: Extra margin added around a display object bounding box to prevent clipping outward visual effects.
terms.detailedDefinition: Effects like `BlurFilter`, `GlowFilter`, and `DropShadowFilter` generate pixels that extend outside the original geometry boundaries. Setting `filter.padding` expands the offscreen RenderTarget dimensions so these blurred edges are not harshly clipped.
terms.whyItMatters: Without padding, blurred sprites appear inside hard square cutoffs matching their original rectangular sprite bounding boxes.

dialogue.user: Why is my drop shadow cut off at the edge of the sprite?
dialogue.aiQuestion: Increase `filter.padding` (e.g. `filter.padding = 20`) to give the offscreen render target enough margin for the shadow!

terms.shortDefinition: A filter technique executing multiple sequential shader stages using ping-pong intermediate textures.
terms.detailedDefinition: Complex effects (such as separable 2D Gaussian blurs or bloom) cannot be calculated in a single shader pass. A multi-pass filter renders pass 1 into texture A, uses texture A as input for pass 2 into texture B, and repeats until the final composite.
terms.whyItMatters: Reduces computational complexity of 2D convolutions from O(N²) to O(2N), turning unplayable lag into smooth 60 FPS rendering.

dialogue.user: Why is a 2-pass blur faster than a single-pass 2D convolution blur?
dialogue.aiQuestion: A separable blur performs a horizontal 1D pass then a vertical 1D pass (N + N samples), rather than an N x N 2D grid of samples per pixel!

terms.shortDefinition: A fast multi-pass box-offset blur algorithm optimized for high performance on mobile GPUs.
terms.detailedDefinition: Kawase Blur applies multiple successive passes with increasing sampling offsets around the center pixel. It yields a smooth, soft blur nearly indistinguishable from Gaussian blur but requires far fewer texture fetches per pass.
terms.whyItMatters: The standard choice for real-time mobile games, UI glassmorphism, and bloom effects where Gaussian blur is too expensive.

dialogue.user: Which blur filter should I use for smooth performance on mobile web?
dialogue.aiQuestion: Use `KawaseBlurFilter` from pixi-filters! It provides smooth blur quality with minimal GPU fillrate overhead.

terms.shortDefinition: A filter using pixel color channels from a map texture to offset the sampling coordinates of the source.
terms.detailedDefinition: DisplacementFilter reads the Red and Green channels of a displacement sprite (e.g. perlin noise or water ripples) and uses those values as (dX, dY) coordinate offsets when sampling the target texture, creating refraction and distortion.
terms.whyItMatters: Enables realistic water ripples, shockwaves, glass refraction, heat haze, and magical warp portals.

dialogue.user: How do I create an animated water ripple effect across a game map?
dialogue.aiThoughts: Describe DisplacementFilter with a scrolling noise sprite.
dialogue.aiQuestion: Create a `DisplacementFilter` pointing to a seamless noise sprite, and increment the displacement sprite position in your Ticker loop!

terms.shortDefinition: A single-pass 5x4 matrix transformation filter for brightness, contrast, hue, saturation, and color grading.
terms.detailedDefinition: ColorMatrixFilter multiplies each pixel RGBA vector by a 5x4 transformation matrix. PixiJS provides built-in presets including `desaturate()`, `sepia()`, `hue()`, `brightness()`, `contrast()`, `night()`, and `predator()`.
terms.whyItMatters: Extremely fast single-pass filter that enables instant screen transitions, damage flashes, night mode tinting, and retro color grading.

dialogue.user: How do I make the whole screen black-and-white when the player dies?
dialogue.aiQuestion: Apply a `ColorMatrixFilter` to your root container and call `filter.desaturate()`!

terms.shortDefinition: A container property that bakes complex child display trees and filters into a single static GPU texture.
terms.detailedDefinition: When `container.cacheAsBitmap = true`, PixiJS renders the container and its active filters once into a private RenderTexture. In subsequent frames, it draws that single cached texture as a normal sprite, bypassing all filter shader calculations.
terms.whyItMatters: Transforms heavy multi-pass filter costs from an ongoing 60 FPS tax into a one-time setup cost for static UI backgrounds and cards.

dialogue.user: My static UI panel has heavy drop shadows and blurs that lag the game. How do I fix it?
dialogue.aiQuestion: Enable `uiContainer.cacheAsBitmap = true`! PixiJS will bake the panel and filters into a single texture and draw it in 1 batched quad.

questions.question: Why does a BlurFilter or DropShadowFilter appear clipped inside a hard rectangle if filter.padding is not set?

choices.text: Because WebGL shaders cannot draw outside the [0, 1] UV texture range
choices.explanation: Shaders can sample texture coordinates freely, but the canvas texture itself is bounded by the target dimensions.

choices.text: Because the default offscreen RenderTarget matches the unpadded bounding box of the sprite
choices.explanation: Correct! Without filter.padding, the offscreen RenderTarget is sized strictly to the sprite bounds, clipping any outward-bleeding blur or shadow pixels.

choices.text: Because the GPU depth buffer discards blurred fragments
choices.explanation: PixiJS 2D rendering does not use standard 3D depth buffer clipping for 2D sprites.

questions.hint: Think about the dimensions of the temporary offscreen RenderTarget.

questions.question: What is the role of the uniform uSampler in a PixiJS fragment shader?

choices.text: It passes the CPU system clock time
choices.explanation: Time values are passed via custom uniform floats.

choices.text: It provides the texture sampler containing the offscreen rendered display object
choices.explanation: Correct! uSampler references the offscreen RenderTarget texture containing the captured display tree pixels.

choices.text: It configures the WebGL blend mode
choices.explanation: Blend modes are managed by the WebGL state machine rather than uSampler.

questions.hint: Think about what image input the shader is processing.

questions.question: Which of the following is a primary characteristic of ColorMatrixFilter?

choices.text: It requires multi-pass ping-pong framebuffers
choices.explanation: ColorMatrixFilter is a single-pass filter with zero ping-pong buffering.

choices.text: It transforms RGBA color vectors using a 5x4 matrix in a single GPU pass
choices.explanation: Correct! ColorMatrixFilter multiplies RGBA vectors by a 5x4 matrix in one fast fragment pass.

choices.text: It samples adjacent pixel neighbors like a convolution blur
choices.explanation: ColorMatrixFilter operates only on the current pixel's color channels.

questions.hint: Consider how many passes and matrix dimensions it uses.

props.title: The FilterSystem Architecture & Lifecycle
paragraphs: PixiJS renders 2D scenes at 60 FPS by batching thousands of textured quads into combined GPU vertex buffers. However, post-processing effects such as blurs, displacement maps, glows, and custom shaders cannot be rendered within the standard batch stream because they require sampling previously rendered pixel regions. To solve this, PixiJS provides the FilterSystem architecture.

When the PixiJS render traversal encounters a DisplayObject or Container with an active filters array, the FilterSystem intercepts normal screen drawing by calling its push() lifecycle method. It computes the axis-aligned bounding box of the display object and expands it by the filter.padding margin. This expansion ensures that outward-bleeding effects, such as a 20-pixel Gaussian blur or a drop shadow, have sufficient offscreen texture canvas and do not get clipped at the original sprite boundary.

Once bounds are computed, the FilterSystem requests a temporary offscreen RenderTarget (a WebGL framebuffer backed by a texture) from its internal RenderTarget pool. Reusing RenderTargets from a pre-allocated pool is critical: allocating fresh WebGL textures every frame causes severe GPU memory fragmentation, driver stalls, and CPU garbage collection pauses. The renderer then redirects its drawing target to this offscreen RenderTarget and renders the container's child hierarchy into it.

After all children are drawn into the offscreen texture, the FilterSystem prepares the filter execution stage. It calculates the uFilterMatrix uniform, a coordinate transformation matrix that accurately maps screen-space quad coordinates into the offscreen texture UV coordinate space [0, 1]. This ensures filters remain visually sharp and distortion-free regardless of display resolution, canvas scaling, or nested container rotations.

The FilterSystem then renders a full-screen quad using the filter's fragment shader. If the filter is a single-pass effect (such as a ColorMatrixFilter or AlphaFilter), the shader samples the offscreen texture uSampler and writes directly to the destination framebuffer. If the filter is a multi-pass effect (such as a 2-pass separable Gaussian blur or Kawase blur), the FilterSystem allocates a second ping-pong RenderTarget from the pool, executes pass 1 (horizontal convolution), swaps the input/output buffers, and executes pass 2 (vertical convolution) before drawing to the destination.

While filters provide immense visual power, they introduce significant GPU performance costs. Every filter pass breaks the continuous sprite batch, switches WebGL framebuffers, and increases GPU memory bandwidth consumption. Applying filters to hundreds of individual sprites can drop framerates from 60 FPS to under 20 FPS. To maintain optimal performance, developers should group related sprites under a single parent Container with one shared filter, utilize fast algorithms like KawaseBlurFilter at half resolution (filter.resolution = 0.5), or enable container.cacheAsBitmap = true for static elements.

primary_goal.prompt: What visual effect or post-processing transformation are you building?

choices.text: Color adjustment, grading, tint, or desaturation
choices.rationale: Color modifications can be performed efficiently in a single shader pass.

choices.text: Blur, glow, drop shadow, or depth-of-field
choices.rationale: Blur and spatial convolutions require multi-pass texture sampling.

choices.text: Water ripples, shockwaves, or optical refraction
choices.rationale: Coordinate distortions are best handled by DisplacementFilter with a map texture.

choices.text: Custom procedural visuals or unique shader math
choices.rationale: Bespoke visuals require writing custom GLSL/WGSL fragment shaders via PIXI.Filter.

choices.text: Simple uniform color tint across a single sprite

node_blur_target.prompt: What is your target deployment platform and update frequency?

choices.text: Mobile devices / 60 FPS continuous real-time animation
choices.rationale: Mobile GPUs have limited fill rate; Kawase blur with reduced resolution maximizes FPS.

choices.rationale: Desktop GPUs can handle full 2-pass Gaussian BlurFilter with high sample quality.

choices.text: Static UI cards, dialog backgrounds, or rarely updated panels

leaf.explanation: ColorMatrixFilter executes a 5x4 matrix multiplication in a single GPU pass. It provides built-in methods like desaturate(), sepia(), hue(), and brightness() without breaking performance.
tradeoffs: Single-pass execution incurs minimal performance penalty
Cannot perform spatial neighboring-pixel blur operations

leaf.recommendation: Use sprite.tint instead of a Filter
leaf.explanation: For simple color tints on individual sprites, setting sprite.tint = 0xFF0000 is processed directly inside the BatchRenderer with zero offscreen RenderTarget overhead.
tradeoffs: Zero batch break overhead and zero offscreen buffer allocation
Multiplicative tinting only; cannot do advanced curves or inverted grading

leaf.explanation: KawaseBlurFilter from pixi-filters delivers smooth blur aesthetics using fewer texture sample taps. Setting filter.resolution = 0.5 cuts GPU fillrate consumption by 75% on mobile devices.
tradeoffs: Blazing 60 FPS performance on low-end mobile devices
Slight softening from bilinear upsampling (usually imperceptible for blurs)

leaf.explanation: Standard BlurFilter implements separable horizontal and vertical Gaussian passes. Setting quality = 3 produces smooth, publication-grade blur gradients on desktop GPUs.
tradeoffs: Requires multiple passes that can slow down mobile web browsers

leaf.explanation: Apply any complex blur or glow filter to the UI container, then set cacheAsBitmap = true. PixiJS renders the filter once into a private texture and draws it as a single quad in subsequent frames.
tradeoffs: Eliminates per-frame filter recalculation entirely (100% batched)
Updating container contents requires invalidating the cache

leaf.recommendation: Use PIXI.DisplacementFilter with a Noise Sprite
leaf.explanation: Create a DisplacementFilter referencing a seamless tileable noise texture. Animate displacementSprite.x and y in your Ticker loop to produce dynamic water ripples and heat haze.
tradeoffs: Requires an extra texture unit and displacement map asset

leaf.explanation: Subclass PIXI.Filter and pass custom GLSL vertex/fragment shader strings and uniform mappings. Update uniform values inside your game loop for dynamic, procedural effects.
tradeoffs: Requires GLSL shader authoring and uniform memory management

cons.description: Forces 50 separate offscreen RenderTarget switch cycles per frame.

cons.title: Severe mobile lag
cons.description: Framerate drops below 20 FPS on mobile devices.

choices.whyThisFits: Only when rendering 1 or 2 highlighted hero characters.
choices.whenToUse: Solo boss highlight or single cursor glow.

choices.label: Grouped Parent Container
choices.description: Group all 50 enemies into one parent Container and attach 1 filter to the container.

pros.title: Single offscreen pass
pros.description: All 50 enemies render into 1 shared RenderTarget before filtering.

cons.title: Uniform parameters
cons.description: All grouped enemies share the same filter intensity.

choices.whyThisFits: Standard best practice for multi-object post-processing.
choices.whenToUse: Particle swarms, enemy mobs, and UI card groups.

steps.title: 2. Blur & Glow Algorithm Selection
steps.description: Choose the mathematical convolution approach for blurs and glows.

choices.label: Multi-Pass Gaussian Blur
choices.description: Standard PIXI.BlurFilter with quality 4 and large kernel radii.

cons.title: High sample taps
cons.description: High texture fetch count increases GPU thermal load on phones.

choices.whyThisFits: High-end desktop gaming and marketing landing pages.
choices.whenToUse: When GPU power is abundant and visual precision is paramount.

choices.label: Kawase Box-Offset Blur
choices.description: Multi-pass KawaseBlurFilter with expanding box sample offsets.

pros.title: Ultra-fast texture sampling
pros.description: Requires far fewer texture reads per pixel pass.

choices.whyThisFits: Production mobile web games and interactive apps.
choices.whenToUse: All mobile-first projects requiring real-time blur or bloom.

steps.title: 3. Static Filter Caching Strategy
steps.description: Determine whether static filtered UI and card assets are cached.

choices.label: Continuous Dynamic Re-execution
choices.description: Execute all filter shader passes every frame even for static UI elements.

pros.title: Always reactive
pros.description: Instantly reflects any child transform or text change.

cons.title: Wasted GPU cycles
cons.description: Calculates identical pixels 60 times per second for unchanging UI.

choices.whyThisFits: Rapidly animating visual effects that change every frame.
choices.whenToUse: Waving water, flickering flames, or animated shockwaves.

choices.label: Bake with cacheAsBitmap = true
choices.description: Bake the filtered container into a static cached texture after initial render.

pros.title: Zero ongoing filter cost
pros.description: Subsequent frames draw the baked texture as 1 standard batched sprite.

pros.title: Restores batch rendering
pros.description: Can be batched alongside regular sprites.

cons.title: Re-bake on mutation
cons.description: Changing child text or layout requires invalidating the bitmap cache.

choices.whyThisFits: Static UI cards, inventory dialogs, HUD backgrounds, and map tiles.
choices.whenToUse: Any filtered object whose contents change infrequently.

steps.title: 4. Filter Resolution & Sampling Scale
steps.description: Configure filter.resolution to balance shader sharpness with GPU fillrate.

choices.label: Native Resolution (1.0x / Retina 2.0x)
choices.description: Render offscreen targets at full native display pixel density.

pros.title: Pixel-perfect sharpness
pros.description: Sharp outlines and fine displacement details.

cons.title: 4x fillrate cost on Retina
cons.description: Huge bandwidth tax on high-DPI smartphone screens.

choices.whyThisFits: Crisp outline filters and fine pixel-art CRT shaders.
choices.whenToUse: Fine geometric effects where blur softness is undesirable.

choices.label: Half Resolution (0.5x Scale)
choices.description: Render offscreen target at half resolution with hardware bilinear upsampling.

pros.title: 75% reduction in pixel fillrate
pros.description: Processes 1/4 the pixel count in the fragment shader.

pros.title: Natural blur smoothing
pros.description: Bilinear upsampling naturally complements blur and bloom.

choices.whyThisFits: Large blurs, glows, bloom, and background depth-of-field.
choices.whenToUse: Mobile devices and performance-sensitive blur/glow effects.

questions.question: What is the primary performance reason that applying individual filters to 100 separate sprites causes severe lag?

choices.text: Each filter requires switching render targets to offscreen framebuffers, breaking sprite batching and causing 100+ separate draw passes
choices.explanation: Correct! Each filtered object forces a framebuffer target switch, vertex flush, and shader draw call, completely destroying the automatic batch renderer.

choices.text: JavaScript garbage collection deletes the texture buffers every frame
choices.explanation: RenderTarget pooling prevents garbage collection, but GPU state switching overhead remains high.

choices.text: GLSL fragment shaders cannot run on more than 16 sprites simultaneously
choices.explanation: GPUs can run millions of fragment shader instances; the bottleneck is CPU-to-GPU state changes and framebuffer bindings.

questions.hint: Consider what happens to WebGL state and draw calls when switching render targets.

questions.question: Why is KawaseBlurFilter preferred over standard multi-pass Gaussian Blur on mobile web devices?

choices.text: Kawase blur runs on the CPU while Gaussian runs on the GPU
choices.explanation: Both algorithms run entirely on the GPU in fragment shaders.

choices.text: Kawase blur uses expanding box sampling offsets, achieving smooth blur quality with significantly fewer texture fetch operations
choices.explanation: Correct! Kawase blur achieves smooth distribution with minimal texture sampling taps, drastically lowering memory bandwidth on mobile GPUs.

choices.text: Kawase blur does not require an offscreen RenderTarget
choices.explanation: Kawase blur still uses offscreen RenderTargets for its ping-pong passes.

questions.hint: Compare the number of texture sample taps required per pixel.

questions.question: How does setting filter.resolution = 0.5 improve mobile shader performance?

choices.text: It renders the offscreen target at half size, reducing fragment shader pixel calculations by 75%
choices.explanation: Correct! Half width and half height means 1/4 the pixel count (75% reduction), with hardware bilinear upsampling smoothing the blur.

choices.text: It drops the framerate to 30 FPS
choices.explanation: It reduces GPU load per frame while keeping the display running at full 60 FPS.

choices.text: It disables the vertex shader entirely
choices.explanation: Vertex shaders are still executed for quad geometry.

questions.hint: Think about pixel fillrate in the fragment shader.

questions.question: When is container.cacheAsBitmap = true the most effective optimization for filtered objects?

choices.text: When the container contains static or infrequently updating visuals, allowing PixiJS to bake the filtered result into a single reusable texture
choices.explanation: Correct! cacheAsBitmap bakes the filtered container into a texture once, drawing it as a single standard batched sprite in subsequent frames.

choices.text: When animating position, rotation, and text at 60 FPS every frame
choices.explanation: Updating children every frame forces expensive re-baking of the cached bitmap, degrading performance.

choices.text: Only when applying shaders to raw WebGL mesh geometries
choices.explanation: cacheAsBitmap works across standard Container trees with sprites, text, graphics, and filters.

questions.hint: Consider how frequently the container visual contents mutate.

questions.question: How does DisplacementFilter calculate coordinate distortion on the target sprite?

choices.text: It uses the Red and Green channels of the map texture to offset the UV sampling coordinates
choices.explanation: Correct! DisplacementFilter maps Red and Green channel values to (dx, dy) coordinate offsets during texture sampling.

choices.text: It physically recalculates the vertex buffer positions on the CPU
choices.explanation: The distortion happens in the GPU fragment shader by offsetting UV sampling coordinates.

choices.text: It inverts the alpha channel of the background canvas
choices.explanation: Alpha inversion is not used for displacement mapping.

questions.hint: Consider what color channels are read from the displacement map texture.

questions.question: Why does FilterSystem lease RenderTargets from a pre-allocated pool instead of instantiating fresh framebuffers?

choices.text: To prevent continuous VRAM allocation churn, memory fragmentation, and JavaScript GC stutter at 60 FPS
choices.explanation: Correct! Dynamic WebGL framebuffer creation triggers severe GC pauses and GPU driver stalls; pooling keeps memory steady.

choices.text: Because WebGL only permits a total of 1 framebuffer in the entire browser context
choices.explanation: WebGL allows multiple framebuffers, but creating and destroying them continuously causes memory churn.

choices.text: Because shaders cannot execute without pre-allocated CSS textures
choices.explanation: RenderTargets are WebGL textures, independent of CSS.

questions.hint: Think about GPU memory fragmentation and garbage collection pauses.
